sections.title: Why plain RAG fails on numbers

items.q: What is the analyst's golden rule Kepler builds on?
items.a: **Never show a number you can't trace** to its source.

items.q: What are the three ways sourced answers still go wrong?
items.a: The **wrong source**, the **right source but wrong number**, and unreliable **mental math**.

items.q: Why is a bare '17' in a 10-K ambiguous?
items.a: It needs **unit, scale and period**: millions or billions, dollars or yen, which year, or even a page number.

items.q: What did Kepler's filter find in plain frontier-model RAG output?
items.a: It refused **10,981 citations**, about **3,810 of them simply wrong numbers**.

items.q: What is Kepler's core architectural rule?
items.a: The **model cites numbers but never writes them**.
Pre-extracted **typed facts** (value, unit, scale, period, source) with **unique IDs**, built from 30M+ SEC documents.
**Deterministic human-written code**, not the model; about a third of citations are math the model didn't do.

items.q: What happens to a number that can't be matched to the registry?
items.a: A post-processing filter **strips it** (or tries a **citation repair**).
**Search wide** with ANN + BM25, fuse to ~60 results, then **trust-weighted re-rank** and a cross-encoder.

items.q: Why can't one source be blindly trusted?
items.a: A call transcript and a 10-K can disagree; that's **information to deconflict**, not a bug.

items.q: How does Kepler stop one desk seeing another's research?
items.a: **Every hit is re-authorized** in Postgres with **scoped tokens** per tenant.
